summary.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques
summary.authors: Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive review and comparative analysis of image denoising techniques, focusing on the preservation of textural information and structural features. The study begins by categorizing image noise into additive and multiplicative types, detailing Gaussian, Salt and Pepper, Speckle, and Brownian noise. It then classifies denoising algorithms into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain). The wavelet domain section is particularly detailed, discussing linear filters, non-linear thresholding (hard, soft, semi-soft, Garrote), non-orthogonal transforms (UDWT, SIWPD), and wavelet coefficient modeling (deterministic and statistical). The core contribution is a quantitative comparison of six specific denoising filters: Mean Filter (MF), Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF), Pixel-Specific Mean Filter (PSMF), Dual-Band Adaptive (DBA), Modified Dual-Band Adaptive (MDBA), and Modified Dual-Band Unsharp Masking Filter (MDBUTMF). These algorithms were tested on a grayscale Lena image with a high noise density of 90%. Performance was evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF). The results indicate that while traditional filters like MF and AMF yield low PSNR values (6.5759 and 8.0603 respectively), the advanced adaptive filters DBA, MDBA, and MDBUTMF significantly outperform them, with MDBUTMF achieving the highest PSNR of 17.9865 and IEF of 16.2066. The paper concludes that the selection of a denoising algorithm is application-dependent and requires knowledge of the specific noise type present in the image. It highlights promising directions for future research in optimizing these adaptive techniques.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a comprehensive review and comparative analysis of image denoising techniques, focusing on the preservation of textural information and structural features. The study begins by categorizing image noise into additive and multiplicative types, detailing Gaussian, Salt and Pepper, Speckle, and Brownian noise. It then classifies denoising algorithms into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain). The wavelet domain section is particularly detailed, discussing linear filters, non-linear thresholding (hard, soft, semi-soft, Garrote), non-orthogonal transforms (UDWT, SIWPD), and wavelet coefficient modeling (deterministic and statistical). The core contribution is a quantitative comparison of six specific denoising filters: Mean Filter (MF), Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF), Pixel-Specific Mean Filter (PSMF), Dual-Band Adaptive (DBA), Modified Dual-Band Adaptive (MDBA), and Modified Dual-Band Unsharp Masking Filter (MDBUTMF). These algorithms were tested on a grayscale Lena image with a high noise density of 90%. Performance was evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF). The results indicate that while traditional filters like MF and AMF yield low PSNR values (6.5759 and 8.0603 respectively), the advanced adaptive filters DBA, MDBA, and MDBUTMF significantly outperform them, with MDBUTMF achieving the highest PSNR of 17.9865 and IEF of 16.2066. The paper concludes that the selection of a denoising algorithm is application-dependent and requires knowledge of the specific noise type present in the image. It highlights promising directions for future research in optimizing these adaptive techniques.

Research Context
Image restoration is a major component of digital image processing. Degradation arises from blurring and noise due to electronic sources. Blurring results from imperfect image formation processes. Noise is introduced during transmission and quantization. Denoising is critical in astronomy, medical imaging, and forensics. Images are represented as 2D arrays of pixel data. Common image types include binary, gray-scale, and color.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The objective is to present an account of noise types and removal algorithms. It is necessary to know the noise type to select the algorithm. The paper classifies noises based on additive and multiplicative nature. A precise classification of potential denoising algorithms is presented. A comparative study of algorithms is conducted for performance evaluation. The study aims to conclude with directions for future research.

Methodological Details
Gaussian noise is evenly distributed over the signal. Gaussian noise follows a bell-shaped probability distribution. Salt and pepper noise is an impulse type of noise. Salt and pepper noise is caused by data transmission errors. Speckle noise is a multiplicative noise in coherent imaging. Speckle noise follows a gamma distribution. Brownian noise is a fractal or 1/f noise. Brownian noise is obtained by integrating white noise. Denoising approaches are divided into spatial and transform domain. Spatial filters are classified into non-linear and linear filters. Non-linear filters remove noise without explicit identification. Linear filters tend to blur sharp edges and details. Wiener filtering requires information about noise and signal spectra. Wavelet based denoising was proposed by Donoho and Johnstone. Spatial-frequency filtering uses low pass filters via FFT. Wavelet domain filtering includes linear and nonlinear methods. Non-linear thresholding exploits wavelet transform properties. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients but creates artifacts. Soft thresholding shrinks coefficients above the threshold. VISU Shrink is a non-adaptive universal threshold. SURE Shrink uses a hybrid of universal and SURE thresholds. Bayes Shrink minimizes the Bayes Risk Estimator function. Cross Validation minimizes the generalized cross validation function. Un-decimated Wavelet Transform provides visually better solutions. Multiwavelets possess short support and higher vanishing moments. Deterministic modeling creates a tree structure of coefficients. Statistical modeling focuses on multi-scale correlation properties. Performance was measured using PSNR and Image Enhancement Factor. Algorithms were applied to a grayscale Lena image. The noise density used for testing was 90%.

Procedures And Architectures
Gaussian noise is modeled with mean and standard deviation. Salt and pepper noise sets pixels to min or max values. Speckle noise arises from random interference of coherent returns. Brownian noise is a non-stationary stochastic process. Spatial filters employ low pass filtering on pixel groups. Wiener filtering implements spatial smoothing via window size. Wavelet transform maps white noise to white noise in domain. Signal energy concentrates in fewer coefficients in transform domain. Hard thresholding removes small coefficients while leaving others. Soft thresholding shrinks coefficients by the threshold value. VISU Shrink threshold depends only on the number of data points. SURE Shrink performs better than VISU Shrink. Bayes Shrink assumes a generalized Gaussian prior. Cross Validation replaces coefficients with weighted neighborhood averages. UDWT is shift invariant and avoids pseudo-Gibbs phenomenon. Shift Invariant Wavelet Packet Decomposition finds the best basis. Multiwavelets are obtained by applying more than one function. Deterministic modeling uses a hierarchical interpretation of decomposition. Statistical modeling exploits local correlation between neighborhood coefficients. PSNR is calculated using Mean Square Error. IEF represents the image enhancement factor.

Key Results
The Mean Filter (MF) achieved a PSNR of 6.5759. The Mean Filter (MF) achieved an IEF of 1.1712. The Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF) achieved a PSNR of 8.0603. The Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF) achieved an IEF of 1.6499. The Pixel-Specific Mean Filter (PSMF) achieved a PSNR of 6.7847. The Pixel-Specific Mean Filter (PSMF) achieved an IEF of 1.2257. The Dual-Band Adaptive (DBA) filter achieved a PSNR of 17.1205. The Dual-Band Adaptive (DBA) filter achieved an IEF of 13.2768. The Modified Dual-Band Adaptive (MDBA) filter achieved a PSNR of 17.2242. The Modified Dual-Band Adaptive (MDBA) filter achieved an IEF of 13.5976. The Modified Dual-Band Unsharp Masking Filter (MDBUTMF) achieved a PSNR of 17.9865. The Modified Dual-Band Unsharp Masking Filter (MDBUTMF) achieved an IEF of 16.2066. MDBUTMF outperformed all other tested filters in both metrics. DBA and MDBA significantly outperformed MF, AMF, and PSMF.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Selection of denoising algorithm is application dependent. Knowledge of noise type is necessary for algorithm selection. Wavelet transform separates signal from noise via energy concentration. Adaptive thresholds generally outperform non-adaptive ones. Shift invariance reduces visual artifacts like pseudo-Gibbs. Multiwavelets enhance performance but increase computation complexity. Statistical modeling aims for exact modeling of image data. High noise levels require spatial configuration analysis.

Contradictions And Limitations
Linear filters blur edges and destroy fine details. Spatial-frequency methods are time consuming. Hard thresholding generates spurious blips or artifacts. VISU Shrink yields overly smoothed images. UDWT adds a large overhead of computations. Wavelet coefficient modeling is computationally expensive. The study only tested on a single Lena image. The noise density was fixed at 90%.

Claims
Advanced adaptive filters like MDBUTMF significantly outperform traditional mean filters in denoising high-noise images. MDBUTMF achieved the highest PSNR of 17.9865. MF achieved a low PSNR of 6.5759. MDBUTMF achieved the highest IEF of 16.2066. The comparison is limited to a single image type. Adaptive methods are preferred for high noise densities.
Wavelet-based methods offer superior noise-signal separation compared to spatial filtering. Wavelet transform maps noise to white noise in domain. Signal energy concentrates in fewer coefficients. Wavelet methods can be computationally expensive. Trade-off exists between quality and computational cost.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Performance was evaluated at a specific noise density. No ablation on different noise types was provided in results.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the Gaussian distribution. Figure 2 illustrates Gaussian noise with different variances. Figure 3 shows the PDF for salt and pepper noise. Figure 4 illustrates salt and pepper noise. Figure 5 shows the Gamma distribution. Figure 6 illustrates speckle noise. Figure 7 shows the Brownian noise distribution. Figure 8 illustrates Brownian noise. Figure 9 shows the expanded classification of denoising techniques. Table 1 compares PSNR and IEF for six filters.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a comparative analysis of six denoising filters. 2. The strongest evidence is MDBUTMF's superior PSNR of 17.9865. 3. The future path involves further research on adaptive algorithms.
